R and Stata side by side

Source: vignettes/articles/r-and-stata.Rmd
r-and-stata.Rmd

The R package and the Stata command implement the same procedure: the same worlds, the same inversion of a target effect into coefficients, the same claims, searches and sweeps. This page matches their functions, arguments, subcommands and options, for readers who move between the two or who want to translate an example.

The same analysis in both

In R:

library(powerape)

d <- ape_dgp(focal = pa_var("program", "binary", p = 0.5),
             covariates = list(pa_var("z", "normal")),
             baseline = 0.30, signal = 0.10)
d <- set_ape(d, target = 0.10)

pw <- ape_power(d, n = 1500, claim = "minimum", sesoi = 0.05, seed = 1)
ape_n(d, power = 0.80, claim = "minimum", sesoi = 0.05, seed = 2)
power_statement(pw)

In Stata:

powerape dgp d, focal(program, binary p(0.5)) covariates((z, normal)) ///
    baseline(0.30) signal(0.10)
powerape setape d, target(0.10)

powerape power d, n(1500) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05) seed(1)
powerape n d, power(0.80) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05) seed(2) engine(mata)
powerape statement

Three things differ by design. The answers agree only up to simulation error, because R and Stata have different random-number generators and the same seed does not give the same simulated studies. In R a design and a result are objects that you keep, print and pass on, whereas in Stata they are stored by name, like estimates store, and the results of the last command are in r(). And in Stata you choose who fits the simulated studies: Stata’s own probit, logit or cfprobit (engine(stata), the default) or a Mata port of the R package’s routine (engine(mata)), which is many times faster and is the one to use for searches.

Describing the world

Probit or logit model = "probit" (default) or "logit" model(probit) (default) or model(logit)
A binary variable pa_var("treat", "binary", p = 0.5) (treat, binary p(0.5))
A normal variable pa_var("age", "normal", mean = 45, sd = 12) (age, normal mean(45) sd(12))
Focal variable focal = pa_var(...) focal(name, ...)
Covariates covariates = list(pa_var(...), pa_var(...)) covariates((name, ...) (name, ...))
Moderator (interaction designs) moderator = pa_var(...) moderator(name, ...)
Latent correlation correlation = 0.2, or a matrix correlation(0.2), or the name of a matrix
Baseline outcome rate baseline = 0.30 baseline(0.30)
Covariate signal (latent pseudo-R²) signal = 0.15 signal(0.15)
Explicit nuisance coefficients gamma = c(...) gamma(numlist)
Integration draws for the truth n_int, seed_int nint(), seedint()
Covariates resampled from pilot data ape_dgp_empirical(data = pilot, focal = "treat", ...) powerape dgp name, empirical focal(treat) covariates(age female) ..., on the data in memory
The world of a fitted pilot model ape_dgp_from_fit(fit, focal = "treat") probit y treat age female, then powerape dgp name, fromfit focal(treat)
Panel: periods, persistence, unit effect ape_dgp_panel(n_periods = 4, rho = 0.3, cre_share = 0.5, ...), pa_var(..., icc = 0.6) powerape dgp name, panel nperiods(4) rho(0.3) creshare(0.5) ..., icc(0.6) in a variable
Unbalanced panel n_periods = c(2, 4, 6) with p_periods, or retention = 0.85 nperiods(2 4 6) with pperiods(), or retention(0.85)
Endogenous focal variable ape_dgp_iv(instruments = ..., endogeneity = 0.4, iv_strength = 0.2, ...) powerape dgp name, iv instruments(...) endogeneity(0.4) ivstrength(0.2) ...
Pin the APE d <- set_ape(d, target = 0.10) powerape setape d, target(0.10)
Pin the AIE set_aie(d, target = 0.08, main_focal = 0.10, main_moderator = 0.03) powerape setaie d, target(0.08) mainfocal(0.10) mainmoderator(0.03)
The true effect of a world true_ape(d), true_aie(d) powerape trueape d, powerape trueaie d
Show a world print(d) powerape describe d

set_ape() returns a new design and leaves d as it was unless you assign the result back; powerape setape changes the stored design in place. To keep two versions in Stata, describe the world twice under two names.

Purpose R Stata

Power at other error rates power_at(pw, alpha = c(0.01, 0.05)) powerape powerat name, alpha(0.01 0.05)

Size at the claim boundary size = TRUE, nsim_size = 500 size nsimsize(500)

Differences worth knowing

Variance estimators. The R package and engine(mata) compute model standard errors from the expected information, robust ones with the HC0 sandwich and clustered ones with the G/(G − 1) factor. engine(stata) uses what Stata reports: the observed information, and its small-sample factors for vce(robust) and vce(cluster). On fixed data the probit standard errors differ by at most about 0.00006 and the logit ones agree to numerical precision, so the two reach the same decision in nearly every simulated study.

Alpha rules. In R a rule is any function of n, for example function(n) alphaN::alphaN(n, BF = 3) from the alphaN package. In Stata it is an expression in @n; alphaN’s rule with BF = 3 is alpharule(chi2tail(1, ln(@n) + 2*ln(3))), which reproduces the R function to machine precision. Justified alpha uses both.

Interaction effects with effects(margins). In Stata the AIE of every simulated study can be computed by ginteff itself (Radean, 2023), which must then be installed from the Stata Journal: net install st0711, from(http://www.stata-journal.com/software/sj23-2). On the control-function route the AIE is computed by margins after cfprobit, with the control function held fixed.

Stata versions. The command needs Stata 16 or later; the control-function route under the default engine uses cfprobit, which needs Stata 18 or later (engine(mata) covers it on any version).

Results are stored by name. Every DGP and every result stays available until you drop it, and the subcommands that work on a result (statement, powerat, alpha) take its name; by default they use the last result.

How the two agree

The Stata command is validated against the R package in four tiers: exact power by enumeration, the estimators on fixed data sets (and against probit, logit, margins, ginteff and cfprobit), the calibration constants, and simulated power, sample sizes and detectable effects in matched designs. See How powerape is validated.

References

Radean, M. (2023). ginteff: A generalized command for computing interaction effects. The Stata Journal, 23(2), 301–335. https://doi.org/10.1177/1536867X231175253
